Real Data: LLM-as-a-Judge (Binary Surrogates)

llm-judge-binary.Rmd

Setup

This vignette mirrors the GPT-4o-mini judge example from ../llm-as-a-judge-debias. We treat the LLM decision Ŷ∈{0,1}\hat{Y}\in\{0,1\} as a binary surrogate for the human label YY, and we plan calibration size and power for the EIF estimator.

Assume we have estimates:

  • Prevalence p=P(Y=1)p = P(Y=1) from pilot human labels
  • Sensitivity q1=P(Ŷ=1∣Y=1)q_1 = P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=1)
  • Specificity q0=P(Ŷ=0∣Y=0)q_0 = P(\hat{Y}=0 \mid Y=0) 
p    <- 0.236
sens <- 0.25
spec <- 0.875
N    <- 5000   # unlabeled/test comparisons

Required calibration size for a win-rate shift

Suppose we want 80%80\% power to detect a Δ=0.05\Delta = 0.05 shift in win rate.

n_req <- power_eif_binary(
  delta = 0.05,
  N     = N,
  m_cal = NULL,
  power = 0.80,
  p     = p,
  sens  = sens,
  spec  = spec
)
n_req
#> [1] 556

With the above numbers, ≈550\approx 550 labeled comparisons are needed for 80%80\% power; using only 100 or 250 labeled comparisons delivers much lower power:

data.frame(
  m_cal = c(100, 250, n_req),
  power = sapply(c(100, 250, n_req), function(m) {
    power_eif_binary(
      delta = 0.05,
      N     = N,
      m_cal = m,
      p     = p,
      sens  = sens,
      spec  = spec
    )
  })
)
#>   m_cal     power
#> 1   100 0.2215246
#> 2   250 0.4686672
#> 3   556 0.8005491

Monte Carlo check 

sim <- simulate_eif_binary(
  R      = 500,
  delta  = 0.05,
  N      = N,
  m_cal  = n_req,
  p      = p,
  sens   = sens,
  spec   = spec,
  seed   = 2025
)
c(empirical = sim$empirical_power, analytical = sim$analytical_power)
#>  empirical analytical 
#>  0.8300000  0.8005491

Using sensitivity/specificity vs. conditional means

If you already have μ̂0=E[Y∣Ŷ=0]\hat\mu_0 = E[Y \mid \hat{Y}=0], μ̂1=E[Y∣Ŷ=1]\hat\mu_1 = E[Y \mid \hat{Y}=1], and pŶp_{\hat{Y}}, you can pass them directly:

power_eif_binary(
  delta = 0.05,
  N     = N,
  m_cal = n_req,
  mu0   = 0.05,
  mu1   = 0.55,
  p_hat = 0.16
)
#> [1] 0.9832705
#> attr(,"theta")
#> [1] 0.13
#> attr(,"p_hat")
#> [1] 0.16
#> attr(,"var_unlabeled")
#> [1] 6.72e-06
#> attr(,"var_cal")
#> [1] 0.0001429856

Either path yields the same variance pieces; choose whichever matches your data summary.
